## Why this page exists

[TODO: opening paragraph — the *why*. Suggested points to weave in, drop,
or replace entirely:]

- Transparency. Users, reviewers, and grant funders deserve to know what
  parts of a scientific tool were authored by a human, what parts by an
  LLM assistant, and what the collaboration loop looked like.
- Not a hype piece, not a confession. The package is open-source and
  test-covered; the question of *who wrote which keystrokes* is
  documentation, not provenance for trust.
- My (Aye's) working hypothesis is that AI-assisted development, when
  driven by a domain expert who reviews every change, produces code that
  is *better* than I would write alone in the same calendar time — more
  tests, more docstrings, fewer copy-paste bugs — without sacrificing
  scientific correctness.

## How to read the per-module estimates

For each subpackage below:

- **Origin** — a one-line note on when and why the module was added.
- **AI involvement** — a rough five-band scale that I (the human author)
  apply by introspection:
  - **None / negligible** — written and maintained by hand.
  - **Light** — Claude suggested a refactor or wrote a docstring; I
    accepted with minor edits.
  - **Moderate** — Claude wrote a substantial draft (one function, one
    test class) that I reviewed and adjusted.
  - **Heavy** — Claude wrote most of the code under my direction; I
    designed the API and verified every behavior.
  - **Co-authored end-to-end** — Multi-session collaboration where the
    design itself was negotiated with the model.

The scale is admittedly fuzzy; treat it as a vibe-check, not a metric.

### `planetarypy.constants` — IAU 2009/2015 + NSSDC fact sheets

- **Origin.** Added in v0.61.0 as a unified planetary-constants API:
  PCK polynomial fields, JPL DE-series GMs, and the NSSDC fact-sheet
  archive composed into a single `Body` object per target.
- **AI involvement.** Heavy / co-authored end-to-end. The PCK +
  NSSDC architecture, the 30-year NSSDC longitudinal archive
  (`parsed_archive.json.gz`), the parser bugfix cycle in v0.64.0
  (J2, range, uncertainty, unit aliases, ten silent-drop fixes), the
  Range / RangeWarning model, the Zenodo lazy-download mechanism
  (v0.65.1) including the cache-key refactor — all developed across
  multi-session Claude Code conversations with the user reviewing
  every change. The 147-test anti-hallucination suite was a
  deliberate guardrail against AI-generated drift.

  with the **API-first / CLI-thin** discipline documented in the
  [CLI how-to](../howto/cli.qmd) — useful logic lives in the library,
  not in `cli.py`.

## Working loop (what the collaboration actually looks like)

[TODO: 2–3 paragraphs on the *practice*. Suggested talking points:]

- Sessions are conversational. You describe a goal; the model proposes
  a design; you accept, redirect, or veto.
- Every change lands as a reviewed commit. No silent autopilot.
- The test suite is the gatekeeper. AI-generated tests are reviewed for
  meaningful coverage, not just line-count.
- Memory: persistent context across sessions captures user preferences
  (semver rules, commit style, "don't bundle scope", help-on-missing
  CLI UX) so the assistant doesn't repeat the same mistakes.
- [TODO: anything about how this differs from a code-completion tool —
  the agent runs tests, edits files, commits, asks clarifying questions.]
